content.comment_body: Imported technical question from a user.

Are you looking to simulate a loss of power? Please refer to the relevant section in the online help documentation (section 3.3.5, power failure). By pressing this button, you can simulate a power outage and observe how the system responds when power is restored. Data marked as retentive will be saved during the interruption, while non-retentive data will not. For example, a retentive counter will resume from its previous value, whereas a non-retentive counter will reset to its initial value, usually zero. You can set data to be retentive by checking the appropriate box for each function. If the device was running before the power interruption, it should resume running upon power restoration. If it was stopped, it will remain stopped.

Hello, thank you for your help. I also want to learn more about this topic. For timers specifically, there are two selectable options: one is a retentive box and the other is a protective activation. You have explained how the retentive feature works, but could you also describe how to use the protective activation button and its intended purpose? Thank you and have a great day.
Protected function blocks cannot be modified in parameter mode anymore. If you display a parameter in a message text, it remains editable. To prevent this, ensure you also protect the message text.

analysis.insight_summary: The discussion focuses on understanding two features within [product_name]: simulating power failure and configuring retentive and protective options for timers and function blocks. The initial reply explains how different data types behave after simulated power loss—important for predicting system behavior after restart. The following exchange shows some confusion about the protective option, later clarified as a way to prevent unintended edits in parameter mode unless the protection is specifically removed from message texts. The conversation highlights the significance of clear documentation and understanding of these features for effective system design and troubleshooting.
